newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Brother's killing intensifies pressure on Bhutto.
newsitem.headline: Brother's killing intensifies pressure on Bhutto.

text.p: Prime Minister Benazir Bhutto faces intense pressure after her brother's death robbed Pakistan's charismatic but ill-fated political dynasty of its last adult male, analysts and newspapers said on Sunday.
Murtaza Bhutto, 42, who had flirted with violence for much of his life, died in a hail of police bullets outside his Karachi home on Friday night. Police say his guards fired first.

The slaying was the latest eruption of violence in Pakistan, whose support role for Western-backed Afghan guerrillas against Soviet occupation in the 1980s placed deadly weapons in the hands of rival ethnic, political and religious groups at home.
Murtaza's supporters and opposition politicians have accused Benazir and her husband, Investment Minister Asif Ali Zardari, of being directly or indirectly responsible for his death.
Benazir, whose government was already under opposition fire for alleged corruption, misrule and economic blunders, must now cope with the political repercussions of a personal tragedy.

Her government had taken pride in what it saw as its success in restoring a semblance of peace to Karachi, Pakistan's biggest city, where a struggle with ethnic militants of the Mohajir National Movement (MQM) cost more than 2,000 lives in 1995.
Now the leeway Benazir gave the security forces against the MQM appears to have rebounded cruelly against her.
"The Karachi police, a creation of the present government, has become a Frankenstein," said The Nation newspaper on Sunday.

It said it would be irresponsible to blame a grieving Benazir for the death of her only surviving brother, but added: "It is inevitable that some of the responsibility for this tragic outcome of the police action would devolve on her."

Dawn newspaper said there was a new priority in Karachi. "It is to check the brutality and trigger-happiness of a police force which has imbibed one overriding lesson from its drive against the MQM: to shoot first and ask questions later."

Last year Murtaza formed a splinter faction of the ruling Pakistan People's Party (PPP) founded by his father, former prime minister Zulfikar Ali Bhutto. He was hanged in 1979 by General Muhammad Zia-ul-Haq, who had toppled him in 1977.
Murtaza spent 16 years in exile, mainly in Syria, at the head of Al-Zulfikar, a clandestine anti-Zia group that was accused of hijacking a Pakistani airliner in 1981.

He returned to Pakistan in late 1993, soon after Benazir regained power, to face charges arising from his underground struggle against Zia. He was freed on bail after seven months. Murtaza's PPP-Shaheed (martyr) Bhutto group posed no threat to his sister's mainstream party, but security officials have said it was suspected of being behind bomb attacks that killed one person and wounded three in Karachi last week. They said his group had backing from Pakistan's arch-rival India.
Murtaza denied the charge just before his death and accused security forces of planting the bombs to discredit him.
Analysts say Benazir will be anxious to prevent his demise from reigniting a damaging family feud that has in the past put her at odds with her thrice-bereaved mother Nusrat.
Nusrat, who has lost her husband and two sons -- her youngest, Shahnawaz, died, apparently of poisoning, in France in 1985 -- has made no public comment on Murtaza's death.
Pakistani commentators say that if she attacks Benazir it could spell trouble for the PPP and its grip on power.
The prime minister, 44, has vowed to complete her five-year term, which expires in October 1998, saying she has no fear of unpopularity arising from harsh but necessary economic measures.
So far Pakistan's powerful military has given no hint that it wants her removed, but her alliance with President Farooq Leghari, an old political supporter, has shown signs of strain.

Leghari chose to air his differences with Bhutto over judicial appointments for the first time on Saturday -- just hours before Murtaza's emotional funeral in the ancestral Bhutto homeland of Larkana, in the southern province of Sindh.
